subject: math
domain: Statistics and Probability — Making Inferences and Justifying Conclusions
cluster: Understand and evaluate random processes underlying statistical experiments
description: Students understand that statistics is the process of using a random sample to make inferences about the parameters of a larger population. They distinguish a population from a sample, a parameter (a fixed numeric characteristic of a population, such as $\mu$ or $p$) from a statistic (a numeric characteristic computed from a sample, such as $\bar{x}$ or $\hat{p}$), and explain why a sample must be randomly selected for the inference to be valid. They reason about how sampling variability and bias affect the trustworthiness of conclusions, and judge whether a claimed inference about a population is justified by the way the sample was collected.
subSkills: Distinguish a population from a sample and identify each in context
Distinguish a parameter (population value: $\mu$, $p$, $\sigma$) from a statistic (sample value: $\bar{x}$, $\hat{p}$, $s$) and assign correct symbols
Explain why random selection is required for a sample to support a valid inference
Identify sources of bias (voluntary response, convenience, undercoverage, nonresponse) that make a sample unrepresentative
Recognize sampling variability: that a statistic changes from sample to sample while the parameter stays fixed
Judge whether an inference about a population is justified given how the sample was selected
Use a sample statistic as a point estimate of the corresponding population parameter

problemArchetypes.name: Population vs. sample identification
problemArchetypes.example: A polling firm surveys $1{,}200$ of the $480{,}000$ registered voters in a county about an upcoming ballot measure. Identify the population and the sample in this study.

problemArchetypes.name: Parameter vs. statistic classification
problemArchetypes.example: Across all $480{,}000$ registered voters, exactly $52\%$ support the measure; in the firm's sample of $1{,}200$ voters, $49\%$ said they support it. Which value is the parameter and which is the statistic, and what symbol ($p$ or $\hat{p}$) represents each?

problemArchetypes.name: Why random sampling matters
problemArchetypes.example: Explain why surveying only voters leaving a single downtown coffee shop would not give a trustworthy estimate of the proportion of all county voters who support the measure.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the source of bias
problemArchetypes.example: A radio host asks listeners to call in and vote on a tax proposal; $73\%$ of the $900$ callers oppose it. Name the type of bias present and explain why the host cannot conclude that $73\%$ of all residents oppose the proposal.

problemArchetypes.name: Sampling variability and point estimates
problemArchetypes.example: Three different random samples of $50$ students give mean study times of $\bar{x}_1 = 6.2$, $\bar{x}_2 = 5.9$, and $\bar{x}_3 = 6.5$ hours per week. Explain why the three means differ even though the population mean $\mu$ is a single fixed number, and give the best single estimate of $\mu$ from sample 1.

problemArchetypes.name: Judge whether an inference is justified
problemArchetypes.example: A researcher randomly selects $200$ households from a city directory and finds $\hat{p} = 0.34$ own a pet. Is it reasonable to infer that about $34\%$ of all households in the city own a pet? Justify your answer in terms of the sampling method.

Easy.description: Single-concept recall and identification from a short, explicit context. The student labels population vs. sample, or classifies a given number as a parameter vs. a statistic, with the random method stated plainly and no competing distractor reasoning. One step, vocabulary-driven.
constraints: Context names the full group and the surveyed subgroup directly
Sampling is stated as random; no bias to detect
Task is to name/identify or match a symbol ($\mu$, $p$, $\bar{x}$, $\hat{p}$), not to evaluate

Medium.description: Two-concept reasoning: the student must both classify (parameter vs. statistic, population vs. sample) and explain a consequence, such as why random selection matters or that a statistic estimates a parameter. Sampling variability is introduced (a statistic changing across samples). Requires a short justification, not just a label.
constraints: Requires choosing the correct symbol AND stating which estimates which ($\hat{p}$ estimates $p$)
May ask why a random sample supports inference while still being clearly random
Introduces multiple sample statistics that differ, testing the fixed-parameter idea
Boundary between tier1 (ends here) and tier2 (begins here)

Hard.description: Evaluation and critique: the student is given a flawed or non-random sampling scenario and must diagnose the specific bias, decide whether the inference is justified, and explain in terms of representativeness and randomness. Multi-step reasoning connecting method to validity, often distinguishing among bias types.
constraints: Sampling method is non-random or biased; student must name the bias type
Requires judging validity of a stated inference and justifying the verdict
May contrast two studies and decide which supports a trustworthy inference

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student swaps population and sample, treating the surveyed subgroup as the whole group
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls the $1{,}200$ surveyed voters the population and the $480{,}000$ registered voters the sample

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses parameter and statistic, attaching the sample symbol to the population value
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels the population proportion $52\%$ as $\hat{p}$ (a statistic) instead of $p$ (a parameter)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student believes a larger sample size overcomes biased selection
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Concludes the call-in poll is trustworthy because it had $900$ responses, ignoring that it is a voluntary-response sample

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks a convenience or voluntary-response sample is acceptable as long as data was collected
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Says the coffee-shop survey validly estimates all voters because real people were asked

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats a sample statistic as the exact population parameter, denying sampling variability
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims the three sample means differing means at least two of them are wrong, rather than reflecting natural sampling variability around a fixed $\mu$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student reverses the direction of inference, using a population fact to describe one sample as if statistics never vary
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Asserts every random sample of voters must show exactly $52\%$ support because that is the population value
